title: Lesson 30: Keeping the Skill Sharp: Staying Current as Tools Change
description: Separating the habits that survive any tool change from the product specifics that go stale, and the small routine that keeps the durable part sharp as everything around it shifts.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Keeping the Skill Sharp: Staying Current as Tools Change", what split does the whole lesson rest on?
options: Durable skills, the habits of judgment that survive any tool change, and perishable details, the product-specific facts that go stale
questions.explanation: The lesson says a good brief written today will still be a good brief after the tool is replaced, while menu positions, button names, current model names, and memory limits are true today and false soon.

questions.question: The lesson says most people who think they lost an AI skill actually lost what?
options: A stack of perishable details: they memorized the wrong version of the tool and stopped checking it
Access to the tools they used before
The ability to write for an audience
questions.explanation: The lesson says the fix is not to re-learn AI but to separate the durable from the perishable, keep updating the perishable, and trust the durable to carry the load.

questions.question: In the lesson's case, what caused Priya's weekly ticket summary routine to degrade?
options: A change to the tone guidance in her brief
A teammate editing her shared prompt
The model behind the tool had been replaced, so summaries came back longer with open issues buried instead of flagged at the top
She stopped including her priority context in the brief
questions.explanation: The lesson uses her case to show that a working routine on top of a changed model is the quietest way a good skill goes bad, because she had not unlearned anything, the tool under her habit had moved.
